title: Transitions and logical order
blurb: Name the relationship between two ideas, choose the transition that signals it, punctuate it correctly, and put sentences in a logical order.
question: “Telehealth visits save patients travel time. ___, they can reduce exposure to illness in crowded waiting rooms.” Does the blank need However, Therefore or Furthermore, and how do you decide without guessing?

teach.body: Formally, a transition is a word or phrase that signals the logical relationship between ideas: addition, contrast, cause and effect, example, comparison, sequence and more. Transitions create coherence, the sense that a paragraph flows in a logical order. Plain English: a transition is a road sign telling the reader what comes next: more of the same, a turn, a result or an example. Choose it by the relationship, never by how formal it sounds.

head: Relationship
Transitions
rows: also, in addition, furthermore, moreover, besides
however, nevertheless, on the other hand, in contrast, instead
therefore, thus, consequently, as a result, so
for example, for instance, to illustrate, specifically
similarly, likewise, in the same way
first, next, then, meanwhile, finally, later
in conclusion, overall, in short, ultimately

steps.label: Check the options
steps.sub: Only one belongs to that family

teach.caption: Name the relationship BEFORE you read the options, so a formal-sounding word cannot pull you off course.
Swap test: replace the transition with and, but, so or such as. If the simple word makes sense, the transition does too.

children.label: Full contrast
children.sub: however, in contrast, on the other hand

teach.caption: Nevertheless fits when the result is surprising given the first idea: “The line was short. Nevertheless, the wait took an hour.”

teach.body: Conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, moreover, consequently) cannot join two sentences with just a comma. Use a period or a semicolon before them and a comma after: “The pharmacy was busy; however, the refill was ready.” Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, so) need only a comma: “..., but the refill was ready.” Subordinators (although, because) start a dependent clause: “Although the pharmacy was busy, the refill was ready.”

rows.label: It rained all week. ___, the picnic moved indoors.
The gym is close to campus. ___, it is cheap.
The quiz was hard. ___, most students passed.
Some foods are rich in iron. ___, beans are.

teach.note: Result: therefore, as a result. Addition: in addition, also. Contrast: however. Example: for example.

teach.body: Nursing applicant Samuel Kim writes: “Telehealth visits save patients travel time. ___, they can reduce exposure to illness in crowded waiting rooms. ___, telehealth is not ideal for every visit, since some conditions need a hands-on exam.” Sentence 2 adds a second benefit in the same direction: Furthermore. Sentence 3 turns against the first two: However. He rejects Therefore for blank 1 because reduced exposure is not caused by saving travel time.

When you must order sentences, look for anchors. A topic sentence or claim comes first. Sequence words (first, next, then, finally) and time phrases (a week later) fix the middle. An example (“For example ...”) comes after the claim it illustrates. A pronoun or pointing phrase (she, these results) must come after the noun it points back to. Check every pair of neighbors, not just the first and last sentences.

teach.text: The most common TEAS trap is an addition transition (Furthermore, Moreover) where the sentences contrast, or a contrast transition (However) where they agree. A second trap is a correct transition with wrong punctuation: “..., however, ...” between two complete sentences is a comma splice.

items: Choose a transition by the logical relationship: addition, contrast, result, example, comparison, sequence.
Name the relationship before reading the options; use the swap test (and, but, so, such as).
Nevertheless and still signal a surprising result; although and granted signal a concession.
Conjunctive adverbs between two sentences take a semicolon or period before and a comma after.
In sentence-order items: claim before example, sequence words in order, noun before pronoun.

summary: You can now name the relationship between two ideas and choose the transition that signals it, using the swap test to check. You can also punctuate transitions correctly and put sentences in a logical order using claims, sequence words and pronoun anchors.

A.q: Which transition best completes the passage? “The clinic extended its evening hours. ___, more patients were able to schedule visits after work.”
A.why: More patients scheduling visits is the effect of the extended hours, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.

whyNot.0: However signals contrast, but the second sentence follows from the first.
whyNot.2: The second sentence is a result, not an example of extended hours.
whyNot.3: Similarly signals a comparison between two parallel things; nothing is being compared.

A.q: Which transition best completes the passage? “Many foods are good sources of potassium. ___, bananas, potatoes, and spinach all contain it.”
A.why: The second sentence names specific foods that illustrate the general claim, so an example transition fits.

whyNot.1: Nothing in the second sentence contradicts the first.
whyNot.2: The foods do not result from the first sentence; they illustrate it.
whyNot.3: The second sentence agrees with the first, so no contrast exists.

A.q: Which transition best completes the passage? “Aaliyah studied for weeks. ___, she felt nervous on the morning of the exam.”
A.why: Feeling nervous is unexpected after weeks of study, so a despite-that contrast transition fits.

whyNot.0: Studying would not cause nervousness, so a result transition is illogical.
whyNot.1: Nervousness is not an example of studying.
whyNot.3: Likewise signals similarity, but the two ideas pull in opposite directions.

B.q: Which transition best completes the passage? “The new scheduling app sends appointment reminders. ___, it lets patients request prescription refills.”
B.why: Requesting refills is a second feature in the same direction as the first, so an addition transition fits.

whyNot.0: On the other hand signals contrast, but both sentences describe helpful features.
whyNot.1: Refill requests are not caused by reminders.
whyNot.2: Nevertheless signals a surprising contrast, but nothing is surprising here.

B.q: Which transition best completes the passage? “Medical assistants must keep patient information private. ___, front-desk staff are required to protect patient records.”
B.why: Both sentences state the same kind of duty for two groups, so a comparison transition fits.

whyNot.1: The duties are alike, not opposite.
whyNot.2: Front-desk staff are not an example of medical assistants.
whyNot.3: The front-desk rule is not caused by the medical assistants' rule.

B.q: Which sentence uses the transition correctly, in both logic and punctuation?
options: The lab closed early, however, the results arrived on time.
The lab closed early; however, the results arrived on time.
The lab closed early; therefore, the results arrived on time.
The lab closed early; for example, the results arrived on time.
B.why: On-time results are a contrast to an early closing, and the semicolon before however and the comma after it are correct.

whyNot.0: Right transition, but only commas join two complete sentences: a comma splice.
whyNot.2: Closing early would not cause on-time results, so therefore is illogical.
whyNot.3: On-time results are not an example of the lab closing early.

C.q: “Night shifts often pay more per hour than day shifts. (1)___, they usually bring fewer interruptions from visitors. (2)___, many nurses find that working nights disrupts their sleep.” Which pair best completes the blanks?
options: On the other hand / In addition
In addition / On the other hand
C.why: Blank 1 adds a second advantage (addition: In addition). Blank 2 turns to a drawback (contrast: On the other hand).

whyNot.0: Reversed: blank 1 adds an advantage, and blank 2 is the contrast.
whyNot.1: Fewer interruptions are not caused by higher pay, and disrupted sleep is not similar to the advantages.
whyNot.3: Fewer interruptions are not an example of higher pay, and disrupted sleep is not a result of fewer interruptions.

C.q: Which word best completes the sentence? “___ the textbook is expensive, it is required for the course.”
C.why: The sentence concedes a drawback (expensive) and then states the opposing fact (required), so a concession word fits.

whyNot.0: Being expensive is not the reason the book is required.
whyNot.2: Therefore cannot begin a dependent clause, and the cost does not cause the requirement.
whyNot.3: Unless makes the requirement depend on the price, which is illogical.

C.q: (A) Finally, she submitted her applications before the deadline. (B) First, Nia researched the nursing programs in her state. (C) Then she requested transcripts to send to those three schools. (D) Next, she chose three of the programs to apply to. Which order is most logical?
C.why: First (B), next she chose three programs (D), then transcripts for “those three schools” (C), finally submission (A). “Those three schools” must come after the three are chosen.

whyNot.0: C refers to “those three schools” before D introduces them.
whyNot.1: First must open the sequence; D cannot come before B.
whyNot.2: Finally must close the sequence, and A cannot come before C.

reteach.title: Transitions are road signs
reteach.question: Driving on an unfamiliar road, you rely on signs: “curve ahead,” “exit,” “road continues.” What would happen if a sign said “straight ahead” right before a sharp turn?

blocks.h: The sign must match the road
blocks.body: Furthermore and in addition are “road continues” signs: more of the same direction. However and nevertheless are “sharp turn” signs. Therefore and as a result are “you have arrived” signs: this is where the last idea leads. For example is a “scenic view” sign: stop and look at a specific case. A wrong sign does not just look odd; it sends the reader the wrong way.

blocks.h: Match the sign to the road

blocks.text: Read the road before you pick the sign: decide the relationship from the two sentences first, then find the option that names it.

explain.body: Before choosing a word, decide how sentence 2 relates to sentence 1: does it add, contrast, result, illustrate, compare or continue a sequence?

test.q: What relationship links these sentences? “The roads were icy. ___, the clinic opened two hours late.”
test.why: The icy roads caused the late opening, so the relationship is cause and effect (therefore, as a result).

whyNot.0: The late opening is expected after icy roads, not opposed to it.
whyNot.2: A late opening is not an example of icy roads.

explain.body: Addition adds another point (in addition, moreover). Example narrows to a specific case (for instance). Comparison links two similar things (similarly, likewise).

test.why: For instance introduces a specific case that illustrates a general statement.

explain.body: If sentence 2 goes against sentence 1, use a contrast word (however). If it follows from sentence 1, use a result word (therefore). Swap in but or so to check.

test.q: Which transition best completes the passage? “The new medication relieved her joint pain. ___, it made her drowsy during the day.”
test.why: Drowsiness is a drawback set against the benefit, so a contrast transition fits (swap test: but).

whyNot.1: Pain relief did not cause drowsiness in the passage, so a result word is illogical.
whyNot.2: A side effect is not similar to pain relief.
whyNot.3: Drowsiness is not an example of pain relief.

explain.body: Between two complete sentences, a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore) needs a semicolon or period before it and a comma after it.

options: The shift was long, therefore, she went to bed early.
The shift was long therefore; she went to bed early.
The shift was long; therefore, she went to bed early.
The shift was long; therefore she, went to bed early.
test.why: A semicolon before therefore joins the two independent clauses, and a comma follows the transition.

whyNot.0: Commas alone cannot join two independent clauses: a comma splice.
whyNot.1: The semicolon must come before therefore, not after it.
whyNot.3: The comma wrongly separates the subject she from its verb went.
